edges.description: Brain enlargement is attributed to white matter edema; the mouse shows megalencephaly together with increased brain water content.
The cysts are fluid-filled spaces in the most swollen subcortical white matter; their formation from the vacuolating process is inferred and has not been studied directly.
Motor impairment is attributed to white matter injury. In the knockout mouse, restoring MLC1 reversed vacuolation and ataxia-like motor deficits together, which supports but does not prove the link.
Pyramidal involvement is attributed to the white matter disease; the intermediate steps are not known.
Late, usually mild cognitive decline is attributed to progressive white matter injury; mechanism unknown.
Coma has followed minor head trauma in genetically confirmed patients.

edges.limitations: Lymphoblasts express MLC1 only at low levels and lack the astrocyte endfoot specialization; the astrocyte arm used knock-down rather than patient alleles.

nodes.description: Experimental. Astrocyte-promoter AAV delivery of human MLC1 reduced cerebellar myelin vacuolation in Mlc1 knockout mice treated before or after onset, and a blood-brain-barrier-crossing vector given to 10-month-old knockout mice normalized MRI water accumulation and reversed locomotor deficits. Overexpression of MLC1 can itself cause vacuolation in mice, so dosing matters. No human data.

evidence.reference_title: Gene therapy rescues brain edema and motor function in a mouse model of megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts.
evidence.snippet: Despite the late-stage intervention, in vivo magnetic resonance imaging revealed normalization of water accumulation. Notably, our therapy successfully reversed locomotor deficits in Mlc1-/- mice

nodes.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous MLC1 variants - nonsense, frameshift, splice-site and missense alleles, the latter affecting residues in predicted transmembrane domains - cause the disease. evidence.snippet: following Ca2+ release, MLC1 binds the Ca2+ effector protein calmodulin (CaM) at the carboxyl terminal where a CaM binding sequence was identified.

evidence.snippet: The mutations further included frameshifts, splice-acceptor mutations, a putative splice-donor mutation, and amino acid substitutions of residues in predicted transmembrane domains. These data provide strong evidence that mutations of MLC1 cause the disease.

evidence.reference_title: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts: Characterization of disease variants.
evidence.snippet: Cysts or near-cystic rarefaction were almost invariably present in both anterior temporal lobes. Additional cysts were located in the frontal and parietal lobes, but never in the occipital lobe.

nodes.description: Minor head trauma can precipitate temporary deterioration with seizures, prolonged unconsciousness and motor decline. Comas lasting days to more than four months have been reported, with full recovery in some patients and permanent worsening in others.

nodes.description: GlialCAM (HGNC symbol HEPACAM) binds MLC1 directly and is required to localize it at astrocytic junctions; GlialCAM is also an auxiliary subunit of the ClC-2 chloride channel. In Mlc1-null mice GlialCAM and ClC-2 are mislocalized and expressed at lower levels, and ClC-2 currents are altered. The human evidence differs: in the post-mortem brain of a p.Ser69Leu homozygote GlialCAM amount and localization were nearly normal. How far loss of the complex, as opposed to loss of MLC1 alone, drives the human disease is therefore unresolved. MLC1 also associates with the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex and Kir4.1 at astrocytic endfeet.

evidence.reference_title: Disrupting MLC1 and GlialCAM and ClC-2 interactions in leukodystrophy entails glial chloride channel dysfunction.
evidence.snippet: Unexpectedly, MLC1 is crucial for proper localization of GlialCAM and ClC-2, and for changing ClC-2 currents.

evidence.reference_title: Mutant GlialCAM causes megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts, benign familial macrocephaly, and macrocephaly with retardation and autism.
evidence.snippet: GlialCAM, an IgG-like cell adhesion molecule that is also called HepaCAM and is encoded by HEPACAM, is a direct MLC1-binding partner.

evidence.reference_title: Mice with megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with cysts: a developmental angle.
evidence.snippet: Mlc1-null astrocytes showed reduced expression of adhesion molecule GlialCAM and chloride channel ClC-2, but no substantial changes in other known MLC1-interacting proteins.

evidence.reference_title: MLC1 is associated with the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex at astrocytic endfeet.

evidence.reference_title: MLC1 is associated with the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex at astrocytic endfeet.
evidence.snippet: We demonstrated a direct protein interaction between MLC1 and Kir4.1.

nodes.description: In two genetic mouse models of MLC, single pyramidal neurons are normal but extracellular potassium dynamics and network activity are abnormal, with spontaneous epileptiform activity and a lowered threshold for induced seizures. A disturbed potassium uptake is proposed to hamper recovery of ion gradients after a seizure, which would fit the frequent status epilepticus in patients.

nodes.description: MLC1 expression is associated with a volume-regulated anion current that is enhanced by hypotonic swelling and abolished by disease-causing mutations or MLC1 knock-down. Patient lymphoblasts and MLC1-deficient astrocytes show hampered regulatory volume decrease, and Mlc1-null astrocytes show slowed regulatory volume decrease that improves on MLC1 re-expression. MLC1 activity is itself tuned by ER calcium release and calmodulin binding.

nodes.description: A spongiform leukoencephalopathy without cortical involvement. Vacuoles are bounded by single myelin lamellae and involve only the outermost lamellae of the sheath, consistent with splitting at the intraperiod line, and fluid accumulates so that white matter water content is greatly increased. Later biopsies show gliosis, enlarged extracellular spaces and fewer, thinly myelinated fibres. The mouse shows more cerebellar and less cerebral hemispheric involvement than patients.

In the post-mortem brain of a patient homozygous for p.Ser69Leu, MLC1 protein was almost undetectable. Truncating alleles remove the protein outright.
